description: BurnSync is developed by an independent, solo-led team, with one member responsible for the project's concept, research, design, development, implementation, and final submission
summary:
BurnSync is a public web app that combines NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from MODIS and VIIRS into one weekly burning-activity calendar for 2000–2026. MODIS carries the record from 2000. VIIRS Suomi NPP is added from 2012, and the latest week uses VIIRS NOAA-20. When both sensors see fire in the same 0.5 degree cell during the same week, the cell is labeled matched. Cells seen by only one sensor stay labeled MODIS only or VIIRS only.

The calendar compares each week with the same week in other years and flags weeks that are above the usual pattern. A separate Prediction view shows that past-years pattern for the coming week. BurnChat uses Gemini to explain the selected week from those numbers.

For responders and land managers, especially in Indonesia, the app shows when burning is unusually active and where the two satellites disagree. The historical map is a sample of eight countries, including Indonesia. A hotspot is a satellite detection. Burned area, smoke, and underground peat fire are outside what this record measures.
details:
BurnSync is a decision-support map for the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge. It reads NASA FIRMS active fire detections and groups them into ISO weeks. A cell of 0.5 degrees is matched only when MODIS and VIIRS both record fire there in that same week. Single-sensor cells stay separate, so the two records are compared instead of being averaged into one number.

The interface opens on those three counts: matched, MODIS only, and VIIRS only. A calendar from 2000 through 2026 shows the MODIS only years before VIIRS and flags a week when its activity is above the usual level for that week of the year. Prediction mode draws the usual pattern from previous years for the coming week. It is a climatology view. BurnChat is a separate explanation tool.

The people it is meant to help are local responders and land managers who need to see a busy week and the places where the satellites disagree, with Indonesia as the worked example. The benefit is a single calendar across the sensor change, with the disagreement left visible.

The historical archive covers eight countries: Australia, Brazil, Canada, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, India, Indonesia, the Russian Federation, and the United States. The latest week is a global seven-day near-real-time feed. VIIRS in the archive is Suomi NPP. VIIRS in that latest feed is NOAA-20. The app states this on the map.

We built it with TypeScript, React, Vite, Leaflet, Python for the FIRMS processing, and Node.js for the site and the chat API. The basemap is Esri World Imagery. The team kept the match rule coarse and visible, kept the sensor names distinct, and kept Prediction separate from the chat so the app does not claim an AI fire forecast.

Super Intelligence Use: Large language models were used to assist with reviewing and refining the interface, server-side components, and submission text. Gemini is integrated into BurnChat to answer questions based on the numerical data from the selected week. No SI-generated images, videos, or audio were used, and no NASA logos or mission marks were generated.
